explanations.answer: Runs ahead and climbs a tree
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Luke 19:4 says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus, since Jesus was about to pass that way. He figured out where Jesus was headed and got there first. A man with a plan and a branch.

explanations.answer: Pushes his way to the front
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any shoving. Luke 19:4 says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him. I think a man too small to see over a crowd would be glad to have a tree. Running ahead and climbing is what the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: Asks the crowd to let him through
explanations.explanation: Nice and polite, but that's not what happened. The text says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him (Luke 19:4). I'd have asked too, honestly, and then I'd have been squished in the back like a cookie at the bottom of the box. Zacchaeus went up instead.

explanations.answer: He must stay at his house today
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Jesus says, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Jesus is the one saying He will stay at Zacchaeus's house. And He says it to the man up in the sycamore tree, who only wanted to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3).

explanations.answer: The crowd is about to block the road
explanations.explanation: The crowd is in the scene, but Jesus never brings it up. His reason is, “…for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Zacchaeus climbed up just to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3). I bet he didn't plan on getting a houseguest.

explanations.answer: He has a message for all of Jericho
explanations.explanation: Jesus is passing through Jericho, but this moment is about one house. He says, “…for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Your house, singular. I think Zacchaeus heard that and nearly fell out of the tree.

Joyfully is it, baker. Luke 19:6 says Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Up in that tree he only wanted to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3). I bet he never expected to be the one doing the welcoming.

I might have been nervous myself, but nervous isn't the word the text uses. Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Joy is how Luke describes the welcome. I'd have been checking my apron for crumbs.

Quiet would've been my guess for a man caught up a tree. But Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. The text tells us the welcome was joyful and says nothing about how loud it was. Quietly isn't a word the verse uses.

explanations.answer: He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. All who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) The grumbling is about the guest list. I think that's a lot of opinions about one visit.

explanations.answer: He has gone to be the guest of a Pharisee
explanations.explanation: Different crowd, different complaint. The grumblers said, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) The text doesn't mention a Pharisee in this scene. The complaint was about Zacchaeus.

explanations.answer: He has passed by the rest of Jericho
explanations.explanation: Creative, baker, and Jesus was passing through Jericho (Luke 19:1). But the people said, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) Nobody in that crowd is griping about being passed by. I think that crowd had a lot to say about who got the dinner invitation.

Half is right, baker. Zacchaeus says, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) A very wealthy man, and half goes out the door. I've given away a cookie before and felt it. This is a whole different level.

A tenth is a number people know well, but it's not the one here. Zacchaeus says, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) Half is a lot bigger than a tenth. He says it standing there, to the Lord.
All would've been something, baker. But Zacchaeus says, “…half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) Half. I won't make it bigger than the text does.

That's right, baker. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Fourfold means he pays back four times the amount. I couldn't even return a borrowed rolling pin on time, so this humbles me.

Half is what he says about his possessions and the poor. For cheating, he says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Fourfold is way more than half. Good mix-up, since both numbers are in the same verse.

The courts never come up in the text. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Nobody is dragging him anywhere. I think a man who offers four times the amount on his own is a man who doesn't need a judge.
Salvation, baker. Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) Today, not someday. It came to the house of the man the crowd was grumbling about.
Judgment sounds serious, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) The word is salvation. And He says it about today.

I can see why you'd think so, since the people were grumbling (Luke 19:7). But Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) The word is salvation, and He says it about this house today.

explanations.answer: This man too is a son of Abraham
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) The people had called Zacchaeus a sinful man (Luke 19:7). Jesus calls him a son of Abraham.

explanations.answer: This man has kept the whole law
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. Jesus gives this reason: “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Jesus doesn't point to a record of any kind. His reason is who Zacchaeus is, a son of Abraham.

explanations.answer: This man was first to see Me
explanations.explanation: Zacchaeus did climb a tree to see Jesus, so I get it. But Jesus's reason is, “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Nothing about being first. If it were a race, I think the tree gave him an edge anyway.

Lost, baker. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) Seek and save. I sat in the back of a drawer for years, so this line gets me every time. Somebody came looking.
I understand why that sounds right, but it isn't the word. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) The word is lost. Zacchaeus just got found, up a tree.

Powerful would fit a man who was wealthy, a chief tax collector (Luke 19:2). But Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) The word is lost, and that's who He came to seek and to save.
